performers: Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux, Maurice Ravel
intro: Ravel conducts the Lamoureux orchestra in Boléro, recorded in 1930. The composer himself presides over the snare drum’s obstinate rhythm and the long parade of soloists.

sections.label: A · Drum, plucked strings and flute
sections.mNote: The first tune begins over C and G

sections.label: B · Solo winds over the drum
sections.mNote: The two tunes pass between exposed solo instruments

sections.label: C · Horn, celesta and woodwinds
sections.mNote: Groups of instruments now share the melody

sections.label: D · Violins join the tune
sections.mNote: Strings and winds carry the melody together

sections.label: E · The turn into E major
sections.mNote: The bass breaks out of its C-major pattern

sections.label: F · Trombone slides and the final chord
sections.mNote: The full orchestra returns to C major

cues.title: The drummer’s two bars
cues.text: A snare drum repeats its two bars over plucked strings. The flute’s first melody moves through C major while the bass stays with C and G. Ravel builds almost the entire piece on this small foundation.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1929), opening; rhythm, bass and flute scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boléro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel on four record sides
cues.text: Ravel conducts the Lamoureux players for Polydor in January 1930. The performance fills four sides of two 78 rpm discs. The long crescendo has to cross three breaks before it reaches its final chord.
cues.evidence: Recording date: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boléro. The BnF catalogue identifies Ravel, the orchestra, two discs and four matrices: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb38509551s.

cues.title: More than one mouth
cues.text: The parade of solitary wind players opens into groups. Ravel combines horn, celesta and two piccolos, then gives the tune to a choir of reeds. The same eighteen-bar phrase now has several players breathing through it.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, ninth and tenth statements. The sequence of instrumental combinations is described at https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violins above the drum
cues.text: The violins join the melody with the woodwinds. Ravel has kept them accompanying for most of the piece; their arrival in the tune broadens it across the orchestra. The drum’s rhythm remains unchanged underneath.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, thirteenth and following statements; violin entries: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boléro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass finally moves
cues.text: The closing passage breaks into E major after the long stay in C. Brass, winds and strings carry the change together. The drum continues through the eight-bar excursion.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 18: E major for eight bars. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boléro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A crash in C
cues.text: Trombones slide, the percussion crashes, and the orchestra recovers C major. The ending takes only a few bars. Nothing in the long crescendo has prepared a gentle departure.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, final six bars: trombone glissandos, bass drum, cymbals, tam-tam and final C-major chord. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boléro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
